title: CCLC Technologies Inc. (Sept 1996 FCA) SR&ED Decision
subject: FCA appeal determining whether provincial funding for coal-liquefaction research was government assistance reducing SR&ED.
outcome: Appeal allowed; FCA reversed FCTD, holding non-commercial government funding constituted government assistance.
summary: Her Majesty the Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527) is the 1996 Federal Court of Appeal ruling that Alberta's payments to CCLC under a Coal Research Agreement were government assistance under the Income Tax Act. For Canadian SR&ED claimants, capped buy-backs and grant-style oversight reduce qualified expenditures and can extinguish refundable investment tax credits.
metaDescription: Read the September 1996 Federal Court of Appeal ruling for CCLC Technologies Inc. regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Dispute and Procedural Posture

The September 19, 1996 judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal in Her Majesty the Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (Court File No. A-801-95; reported at 96 D.T.C. 6527, 139 D.L.R. (4th) 765, [1996] 3 C.T.C. 246, and [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226) stands as a foundational pillar of Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax jurisprudence. Heard in Vancouver, British Columbia, before an appellate panel comprising Justices Hugessen, Strayer, and Desjardins, with the unanimous oral judgment delivered from the bench by Justice Strayer, the ruling reversed the November 10, 1995 judgment of Justice Rouleau of the Federal Court of Canada, Trial Division (Action No. T-3457-90; 95 D.T.C. 5685, [1996] 1 C.T.C. 7, 103 F.T.R. 292). The taxpayer's subsequent application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada (File No. 25631) was dismissed on June 19, 1997, cementing the Federal Court of Appeal's holding as the definitive judicial standard across Canada for distinguishing bona fide commercial transactions from "government assistance" under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act").

At the core of the litigation was a Notice of Reassessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") on November 10, 1989, and confirmed on December 14, 1990, in respect of the 1987 taxation year of CCLC Technologies Inc. ("CCLC"). In its 1987 corporate tax return, CCLC claimed deductions for current and capital SR&ED expenditures totaling $2,298,359 and sought a corresponding refundable Investment Tax Credit ("ITC"). The Minister disallowed the refundable ITC and reassessed CCLC on the ground that $2,290,317 in financial inflows received and receivable by CCLC from the Government of the Province of Alberta pursuant to a "Coal Research Agreement" constituted "government assistance" in the nature of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, or other form of assistance under paragraph 12(1)(x) and subsections 127(9) and 127(11.1)(c) of the Act. Characterization of the provincial funding as government assistance triggered two severe, interrelated statutory consequences: first, it reduced CCLC's "qualified expenditure" pool almost dollar-for-dollar, effectively extinguishing its entitlement to refundable SR&ED ITCs; second, to the extent that the assistance did not already reduce deductible SR&ED expenditure pools, it mandated an income inclusion in computing CCLC's taxable income from a business or property under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
Factual Matrix and the Coal Research Agreement

CCLC Technologies Inc. was an Alberta corporation formed through the statutory amalgamation of Canadian Coal Liquefaction Corporation and Contar Systems Engineering Ltd., operating as a specialized industrial research and engineering enterprise. In the early 1980s, Dr. Fritz Boehm, President of Contar Systems Engineering Ltd., conceived an ambitious technological program aimed at developing a dual-process reactor technology capable of simultaneously converting sub-bituminous coal and heavy oil (bitumen) feedstocks into synthetic light crude oil through integrated liquefaction and catalytic upgrading. Because scaling the dual-process liquefaction concept from bench-scale experimentation to an industrial process demonstration unit required projected capital outlays of approximately $100 million alongside institutional credibility within the petroleum sector, CCLC solicited the financial and technical participation of the Province of Alberta. Following eleven months of intensive technical and legal negotiations, CCLC and Her Majesty the Queen in right of the Province of Alberta executed the Coal Research Agreement on April 1, 1986.

The Coal Research Agreement was structured as a complex, hybrid technology development arrangement weaving together intellectual property cross-licensing, joint governance, interim co-ownership, and contingent buyout provisions. Under the preamble (Paragraph 7) and operative clauses of the contract, both CCLC and the Province of Alberta sought to advance coal-oil co-processing technology based on pooled technical know-how. Existing background technologies, specialized equipment, technical personnel, and intellectual property owned separately by CCLC and the province were pooled and cross-licensed into the project, supplemented by foundational coal liquefaction technology licensed from a German industrial firm. Paragraphs 4 and 5(6) of the agreement established a joint Project Management Committee comprising representatives of both CCLC and the Province of Alberta. Through this committee, provincial officials participated in defining technical scopes, project schedules, and operational budgets, actively monitored experimental progress, and retained the contractual right to withhold scheduled financial disbursements if CCLC failed to satisfy corporate liabilities as they fell due.

With respect to proprietary rights and financial returns, Paragraphs 10, 11, and 12 of the Coal Research Agreement granted the Province of Alberta and CCLC an undivided 50/50 joint ownership interest in all foreground project technology pending commercialization. Crucially, the agreement bifurcated the ultimate disposition of the Province of Alberta's 50% undivided property interest based on whether the research achieved commercial viability. If the co-processing technology achieved commercialization, the Province of Alberta was contractually obligated to sell its 50% equity and property stake back to CCLC for a price capped strictly at the return of the province's principal monetary contribution plus interest costs, payable via a formula-based royalty out of gross commercial revenues. Conversely, if commercialization was not achieved, the mandatory buy-back did not trigger; instead, the Province of Alberta was entitled to nothing except its 50% undivided equity interest in a technology demonstrated not to have present commercial value. Finally, Paragraph 18 of the Coal Research Agreement explicitly stipulated that nothing in the contract was to be construed as creating a legal partnership, joint venture, or agency relationship between the Province of Alberta and CCLC.

body.text: During its 1987 taxation year, CCLC incurred $1,102,889 in current SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and $1,195,470 in capital SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b), totaling $2,298,359. In that same taxation year, CCLC received cash disbursements of $725,569 from the Province of Alberta and accrued an enforceable entitlement to receive a further $1,564,748 at year-end, aggregating $2,290,317. Throughout the 1987 taxation year and the relevant assessment period, the dual-process coal liquefaction technology was never successfully commercialized and demonstrated no present commercial value.
Governing Statutory Framework Under the Income Tax Act

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive regime operates on a core legislative principle implemented by Parliament: tax incentives, whether delivered through immediate expenditure deductions under section 37 or Investment Tax Credits under section 127, are designed to subsidize only the net out-of-pocket financial risk borne by a taxpayer performing SR&ED in Canada. To prevent double-dipping—whereby a corporation receives direct public grants or subsidies to fund R&D and simultaneously claims federal ITCs on the gross, unreduced expenditure base—the Act integrates the income inclusion rules in Part I (Division B) with the SR&ED expenditure pool rules and ITC calculation provisions.

In the 1987 taxation year at issue in CCLC Technologies (and continuing in substantive structure under the contemporary Act), four interlocking statutory provisions governed the dispute. First, subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) mandates that a taxpayer include in computing income from a business or property for a taxation year any amount (other than a prescribed amount) received by the taxpayer in the year, in the course of earning income from a business or property, from a government, municipality, or other public authority (subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ii)) where the amount can reasonably be considered to have been received "as a reimbursement, contribution, allowance or as assistance, whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance, in respect of the cost of property or in respect of an expense". Second, subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) establishes a statutory carve-out: an amount otherwise captured as assistance under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) is included in income only to the extent that the amount "may not reasonably be considered to be a payment made in respect of the acquisition by the payor or the public authority of an interest in the taxpayer, his business or his property"; conversely, an amount that may reasonably be considered to be such a payment is excluded from income inclusion. Where a government body acts as a bona fide equity investor or property purchaser acquiring an enduring proprietary interest in the taxpayer's business or assets, the capital inflow is excluded from paragraph 12(1)(x).

Third, paragraphs 37(1)(a), 37(1)(b), and 37(1)(d) govern the cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada. In 1987, paragraph 37(1)(a) governed current SR&ED expenditures and paragraph 37(1)(b) governed capital SR&ED expenditures (capital expenditures made after 2013 were later excluded from the SR&ED incentives, and their eligibility has since been restored for property acquired after December 15, 2024). Paragraph 37(1)(d) reduces the taxpayer's deductible section 37 SR&ED pool by any government assistance or non-government assistance received in respect of SR&ED expenditures claimed in the pool. Under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(v), paragraph 12(1)(x) sweeps assistance into taxable income to the extent that it does not otherwise reduce the cost of property or reduce deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d). Fourth, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and paragraph 127(11.1)(c) govern Investment Tax Credits and the reduction of qualified expenditures. Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of an ITC from Part I tax otherwise payable, while subsection 127(9) defines "government assistance" broadly as "assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance or as any other form of assistance". In the 1987 taxation year, paragraph 127(11.1)(c) (the statutory predecessor to modern subsection 127(18) and paragraph (h) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9)) stipulated that the amount of a "qualified expenditure" made by a taxpayer in a taxation year for SR&ED must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that, at the time of filing the return of income for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the expenditure.
Divergence Between the Trial Division and the Federal Court of Appeal

When CCLC appealed the Minister's reassessment to the Federal Court of Canada, Trial Division, Justice Rouleau allowed the taxpayer's appeal and vacated the reassessment. The Trial Division anchored its analysis in three foundational Canadian tax authorities: Ottawa Valley Power Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue, [1969] C.T.C. 242 (Ex. Ct.), aff'd [1970] S.C.R. 941; G.T.E. Sylvania Canada Limited v. The Queen, 74 D.T.C. 6315; and The Queen v. Consumers' Gas Company Ltd., [1987] 2 F.C. 60, [1987] 1 C.T.C. 79, 87 D.T.C. 5008 (F.C.A.). Justice Rouleau observed that in Consumers' Gas, Justice Hugessen had remarked that the statutory term "assistance" carries with it "the colour of a grant or subsidy". Focusing on the operational mechanics of the Coal Research Agreement, Justice Rouleau concluded that the Province of Alberta lacked "donative intention" and was instead acting as an active commercial participant. The trial judge emphasized that the contract resulted from eleven months of tough negotiations, involved the mutual pooling of background intellectual property, granted Alberta an interim 50% undivided co-ownership interest in the technology, and placed provincial representatives on the Project Management Committee with authority to withhold funds if corporate liabilities went unpaid. Dismissing the Crown's reliance on Paragraph 18 (which disclaimed any partnership or joint venture) as overly simplistic under the principle in Weiner v. Harris, [1910] 1 K.B. 285, the Trial Division ruled that the payments flowed from an ordinary commercial business arrangement and therefore fell outside subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x).

On appeal by the Crown, the Federal Court of Appeal dismantled the Trial Division's legal analysis and reversed the judgment in its entirety. Delivering oral judgment for the Court, Justice Strayer framed the appeal around two decisive questions: first, whether the amounts provided by the Government of Alberta to CCLC constituted "assistance" as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or as any other form of assistance within the meaning of subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) and subsections 127(9) and 127(11.1) of the Act; and second, if the answer to the first question was in the affirmative, whether such amounts should nevertheless be excluded from income pursuant to subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) as a payment made in respect of the acquisition by the payor of an interest in the taxpayer, its business, or its property. Answering the first question in the affirmative and the second in the negative, the Federal Court of Appeal held that Justice Rouleau had misconstrued the Coal Research Agreement under which the payments were made and erred in the application to it of the relevant provisions of the Act. Justice Strayer clarified that when Consumers' Gas contrasted "government assistance" with payments made by public authorities "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the interests of the payor," the Court of Appeal was speaking strictly of advancing the business interests of the payor—not broad socio-economic or public policy mandates to foster industrial research within a province.
Final Holding and Jurisprudential Legacy in Canada

The Federal Court of Appeal held that the Coal Research Agreement bore none of the economic hallmarks of an ordinary business arrangement. Because the Province of Alberta was required to sell its 50% interest back to CCLC for nothing more than the return of its money contribution plus its interest costs if the project proved commercially successful, and was entitled to nothing except an equity interest in a technology demonstrated not to have present commercial value if the project did not prove to have commercial value, the province could not receive any net profit if the venture succeeded and would gain an equity interest only if the venture proved uncommercial. As the Court observed, a business that invested money in ventures on the basis that it could not receive any net profit if the venture succeeded, and would gain an equity interest only if the venture proved uncommercial, would not long survive. Furthermore, the Court ruled that the province's surveillance and participation on the Project Management Committee did not transform the funding into a commercial venture; rather, such oversight was "at least equally consistent with the role of a prudent grant-giver assuring itself that its contribution was being spent as intended". Finally, because commercial success would have stripped Alberta of any lasting property rights in a going concern through the mandatory buy-back, the payments could not qualify as a property or equity acquisition under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii). The Crown's appeal was allowed with costs, the judgment of the Trial Division was set aside, and CCLC's action was dismissed with costs.

In the decades following September 1996, the CCLC Technologies analytical framework—applied by Canadian tax courts and the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA")—has served as the controlling legal standard for evaluating government funding arrangements in the SR&ED context. It is reflected in the CRA's administrative guidelines (Assistance and Contract Payments Policy) and was directly applied by the Federal Court of Appeal in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196 (holding that interest-free, conditionally repayable contributions from the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency constituted government assistance) and in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178, leave to appeal refused (S.C.C. May 25, 2023) (holding that even unconditionally repayable government loans under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative constituted government assistance where the financing terms were not strictly commercial—a ruling so sweeping that it prompted the Department of Finance in the November 21, 2023 Fall Economic Statement to introduce specific statutory exceptions for bona fide repayable public loans).
Core Legal, Contractual, and Evidentiary Failures

Unlike routine SR&ED disputes that turn on whether the taxpayer's technical activities satisfy the three-part scientific eligibility criteria under subsection 248(1) of the Act (technological uncertainty, systematic investigation or search, and technological advancement), the Crown in CCLC Technologies did not dispute that CCLC's coal-and-heavy-oil co-processing work constituted eligible SR&ED. Rather, CCLC's complete disqualification from refundable ITCs resulted from fatal legal, contractual, and economic structuring failures in how its research funding and intellectual property rights were documented and executed. A rigorous decomposition of the appellate judgment reveals five interconnected deficiencies that doomed the taxpayer's claim.
Asymmetrical Risk-Reward Mechanics and the Absence of Ordinary Commercial Animus

The primary legal deficiency in CCLC's position was its inability to satisfy the commercial animus standard established in Consumers' Gas and refined by Justice Strayer. In Ottawa Valley Power and Consumers' Gas, payments made by public authorities to private utilities (to convert electrical frequency systems from twenty-five cycle to sixty cycle power or to relocate gas mains) were held not to be government assistance because the public authority was acting strictly as a commercial counterparty protecting or advancing its own operational business assets for commensurate commercial consideration. CCLC attempted to shelter under this jurisprudence by arguing that the Province of Alberta entered into the Coal Research Agreement with business animus to exploit provincial coal and heavy oil reserves. However, the Federal Court of Appeal examined the substantive economic return mechanics built into Paragraphs 10, 11, and 12 of the Coal Research Agreement and exposed a fatal structural asymmetry between risk and reward.

Under the contract's upside branch, if CCLC overcame the technological uncertainties and the dual-process liquefaction technology proved commercially viable, the Province of Alberta was legally obligated to transfer its 50% undivided interest back to CCLC in exchange for a payout capped at the province's nominal cash contribution plus interest costs. The province was contractually barred from participating in any net enterprise profit, equity appreciation, or uncapped commercial royalty stream commensurate with early-stage technological risk. Conversely, under the contract's downside branch, if the SR&ED program failed to yield a commercially viable process (which was the factual reality during the 1987 taxation year), CCLC had no obligation to repay the $2,290,317 contributed by the province. Instead, the province was left holding a 50% undivided co-ownership interest in uncommercialized technical data and patents that possessed no demonstrated market value.

Justice Strayer highlighted the economic impossibility of characterizing this structure as an "ordinary business arrangement". In private capital markets, an arm's-length venture investor or commercial co-developer funding high-risk, pre-commercial SR&ED demands an uncapped equity return or high-multiple royalty upside specifically to compensate for the high probability of total capital loss upon technical failure. By drafting an agreement where the funder bore 100% of the downside risk of non-commercialization while being contractually restricted to a zero-net-profit return (principal plus interest cost recovery) upon success, CCLC created an instrument that no private commercial actor would ever execute to advance its own business interests. Consequently, the payments were driven by public policy animus—subsidizing industrial R&D in Alberta—and fell squarely within the broad statutory sweep of "any other form of assistance" in subsection 127(9) and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).
The Mandatory Buy-Back Cap and Disqualification Under Subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii)

CCLC's second major legal failure occurred in its alternative defence under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) of the Act. Even where a payment from a public authority exhibits features of financial assistance under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv), subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) excludes the payment from income inclusion (and by extension informs the capital character of the receipt) to the extent that the payment may reasonably be considered to be a payment made in respect of the acquisition by the payor or the public authority of an interest in the taxpayer, his business or his property, because the subparagraph includes in income only an amount that "may not reasonably be considered to be made in respect of the acquisition" of such an interest. The Coal Research Agreement gave the Province of Alberta a 50% undivided co-ownership interest in the foreground project technology, and CCLC contended that the $2,290,317 paid and payable in 1987 was consideration for the province's acquisition of an interest in CCLC's intellectual property.

The Federal Court of Appeal pierced this formalistic conveyancing structure by evaluating the durability and economic substance of the property interest across both contingent branches of the contract. Had the research project succeeded, the mandatory buy-back clause stripped the Province of Alberta of its 50% ownership stake automatically upon repayment of principal plus interest costs. As Justice Strayer held, if the project had been successful, the government "would have acquired no lasting property rights in a going concern". A temporary interest that the government would be obliged to sell back for merely a return of its money contributions plus interest the moment the project proved commercially successful does not constitute the acquisition of lasting property rights; in the Court's words, the contribution if anything became of the nature of a grant, subsidy, or forgivable loan and cannot reasonably be considered a payment for the purpose of acquisition of property. Conversely, because the project failed to achieve commercial viability during the relevant period, the mandatory buy-back was not triggered, leaving Alberta with a half-share in unproven technology lacking demonstrated commercial value. Acquiring a default residual title in an uncommercialized R&D failure cannot reasonably be characterized as the commercial acquisition of property for the purposes of subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii). Thus, the contractual coupling of interim 50/50 IP co-ownership with a mandatory, capped redemption upon commercialization destroyed CCLC's ability to invoke the subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) property acquisition exemption.
The Prudent Grant-Giver Doctrine: Misinterpreting Technical Governance and Project Surveillance

A critical evidentiary miscalculation made by CCLC—and initially accepted by the Trial Division—was relying heavily on the Province of Alberta's extensive technical involvement and administrative oversight to prove the existence of a commercial joint venture. At trial, CCLC adduced extensive evidence showing that provincial representatives sat on the Project Management Committee, negotiated technical parameters over eleven months, contributed background provincial IP and personnel, reviewed experimental milestones, and held contractual authority under Paragraph 5(6) to withhold funding tranches if CCLC failed to pay its corporate creditors.

In Paragraph 6 of the appellate decision, Justice Strayer established what has become known in Canadian SR&ED practice as the prudent grant-giver doctrine. The Federal Court of Appeal ruled that the various forms of surveillance of, or participation in, the management of the project by the Government's representatives, as contemplated by the agreement, did not indicate any commercial role of the Government and were "at least equally consistent with the role of a prudent grant-giver assuring itself that its contribution was being spent as intended". Public authorities dispensing millions of dollars in taxpayer-funded grants or conditionally repayable subsidies routinely impose strict project governance, audit rights, technical steering committees, and solvency covenants to prevent misappropriation or waste of public funds. Because such administrative and technical oversight is at least equally consistent with public grant administration, the Federal Court of Appeal was not persuaded that it indicated any commercial role of the Government, and it therefore did not displace the characterization of the payments as "government assistance".
Impact of Non-Commercialization and Accrual of Receivable Assistance on SR&ED Expenditure Pools

Two further technical and accounting dimensions of the 1987 taxation year compounded CCLC's failure. In Paragraph 5 of the judgment, Justice Strayer noted that the government payments under the Coal Research Agreement "became, in the circumstances of non-commercialization of the technology, a grant, subsidy, a forgivable loan, or similar form of assistance" under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) and subsection 127(9). Because the province would recover its money contribution plus its interest costs only by selling its interest to CCLC if the project proved commercially successful, and because the project did not prove to have commercial value during the period in question, CCLC had no obligation to return the province's contribution during the taxation year. Under Canadian tax law, a funding advance whose repayment is contingent on uncertain future commercial revenues operates functionally as a forgivable loan or conditionally repayable grant until the contingency is satisfied.

Furthermore, in 1987, CCLC actually received $725,569 in cash from Alberta, but was also entitled to receive an additional $1,564,748 at year-end under the agreement's billing milestones. Under paragraph 127(11.1)(c) (and modern subsection 127(18)), qualified SR&ED expenditures are reduced not merely by assistance received in cash, but also by assistance the taxpayer is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive at the time of filing the income tax return for the year. By incurring $2,298,359 in SR&ED expenditures within the exact same corporate entity and project boundary that accrued $2,290,317 in provincial assistance ($725,569 received plus $1,564,748 receivable), CCLC caused 99.65% of its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool to be eliminated in real time on an accrual basis.
Contractual Labeling Versus Substantive Economic Reality

Finally, the litigation exposed the danger of contradictory contractual drafting in R&D collaborative agreements. In Paragraph 18 of the Coal Research Agreement, the parties included a standard liability-shielding boilerplate clause declaring that nothing in the agreement created a partnership, joint venture, or agency relationship. While the Trial Division brushed aside Paragraph 18 on the principle that parties cannot alter the legal nature of their relationship merely by mislabeling it, the Federal Court of Appeal looked to the substantive economic rights across the entire contract. A fundamental contradiction pervaded CCLC's litigation posture: CCLC asked the courts to ignore its own express contractual disclaimer of a joint venture in Paragraph 18, while simultaneously asking the courts to respect the formalistic label of "co-ownership of property" in Paragraph 10 without examining the mandatory buy-back in Paragraph 11 that gutted the economic substance of that property ownership. The appellate decision did not rely on Paragraph 18 or on the parties' labels; it examined what the agreement provided in substance—an obligation on the province to sell its interest for a return of its money contribution plus interest costs if the project succeeded, and only an equity interest in a technology without demonstrated commercial value if it did not.
Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements, Taxpayer Failures, and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement governing SR&ED government assistance and property acquisition exclusions in Canada against the specific contractual and evidentiary failures of CCLC Technologies Inc. and the controlling standard of proof established by the Federal Court of Appeal.

headers: Taxpayer's Contractual / Evidentiary Failure in CCLC Technologies Inc.
Federal Court of Appeal's Governing Standard of Proof

cells: Subsection 127(9) & Subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) (Income Tax Act) — Exclusion of "Ordinary Business Arrangements" from "Government Assistance" To escape characterization as "government assistance" (grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, or any other form of assistance), funds provided by a public authority must be advanced pursuant to an ordinary commercial transaction driven by business animus (Consumers' Gas; Ottawa Valley Power).

CCLC executed the Coal Research Agreement under which the Province of Alberta funded $2,290,317 in 1987 (received and receivable). However, Paragraphs 10–12 required Alberta to sell its 50% stake back to CCLC upon commercialization for only its principal contribution plus interest costs (zero net profit), while leaving Alberta with nothing except a 50% equity interest in a technology demonstrated not to have present commercial value if the project did not prove commercially successful.

The Commercial Animus & Symmetrical Risk-Reward Test: To fall outside "government assistance," payments by a public authority must be made "in exactly the same way for exactly the same reasons as payments made by private business, that is, for the purpose of advancing the interests of the payor," which the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed refers to the business interests of the payor. An arrangement under which the payor could not receive any net profit if the venture succeeded, and would gain an equity interest only if the venture proved uncommercial, is not an arrangement that a business would enter into to advance its business interests.

Subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) (Income Tax Act) — Exclusion for Acquisition of an Interest in the Taxpayer, its Business, or its Property Payments from a public authority are excluded from paragraph 12(1)(x) assistance if they can reasonably be considered payments made to acquire a bona fide proprietary or equity interest in the taxpayer, its business, or its property.

CCLC granted Alberta an interim 50/50 undivided co-ownership interest in the foreground technology. However, the mandatory buy-back clause forced Alberta to relinquish that property interest upon commercialization in exchange for a capped return of principal and interest, depriving the province of any enduring ownership in a commercialized asset.

The Lasting Property Rights in a Going Concern Standard: To satisfy subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii), the taxpayer must demonstrate that the public authority acquires lasting property rights in a going concern or enduring commercial asset. A defeasible title that is automatically extinguished via a mandatory cost-plus-interest buy-back if the project succeeds—or that leaves the government holding a half-share in a technology without demonstrated commercial value if it fails—cannot reasonably be considered a payment for the purpose of acquisition of property; the contribution, if anything, is of the nature of a grant, subsidy, or forgivable loan.

Jurisprudential Evidentiary Standard — Refuting Donative / Subsidy Intent via Joint Project Governance Taxpayers seeking to prove a commercial joint venture or co-development relationship must establish that shared management reflects commercial co-venturing rather than grant compliance monitoring.

CCLC relied heavily on evidence of 11 months of contract negotiations, pooling of background IP, provincial seats on the Project Management Committee, technical surveillance, and Paragraph 5(6) payment-withholding rights to argue Alberta acted as a commercial partner.

The "Prudent Grant-Giver" Doctrine: Evidence of government technical surveillance, steering committee participation, milestone vetting, and financial withholding covenants does not, in itself, indicate any commercial role of the government. Such oversight is "at least equally consistent with the role of a prudent grant-giver assuring itself that its contribution was being spent as intended".

Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 127(11.1)(c) [Modern Subsection 127(18)] — Treatment of Conditionally Repayable Funding & Non-Commercialization Funding whose repayment is contingent upon future commercial revenues reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures as a "forgivable loan" or "other form of assistance" unless unconditional, commercial repayment terms exist.

The return of Alberta's money contribution plus interest costs was contingent on the project proving commercially successful, in which case Alberta would be obliged to sell its interest to CCLC for that price. Because the coal liquefaction technology did not prove to have commercial value during the period in question, no obligation to return Alberta's contribution crystallized.

Substantive Contingency & Economic Reality Standard: Where repayment is conditional upon achieving technical commercialization or revenue thresholds, and commercialization is not achieved in the taxation year, the advances constitute a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, or similar assistance. Even where repayment is unconditional, the terms as a whole must reflect strictly commercial market rates and risk allocation (CAE Inc.).

Paragraph 127(11.1)(c) [Modern Subsection 127(18)] & Paragraph 37(1)(d) — Accrual Recognition and Pool Reduction Qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by all assistance "received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received" at the tax filing deadline.

CCLC incurred $2,298,359 in SR&ED expenditures in 1987 inside the same corporate and project structure that received $725,569 in cash and accrued $1,564,748 in year-end receivables from Alberta, resulting in an immediate $2,290,317 reduction of its qualified expenditure base.

Strict Accrual Matching to SR&ED Expenditures: Once an enforceable right to receive assistance accrues under contract milestones ("entitled to receive"), the full receivable amount immediately grinds down the taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes under section 127 and reduces the deductible section 37 expenditure pool (or triggers income inclusion under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv)).

body.text: Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of CCLC Technologies Inc. (and its direct progeny in Immunovaccine Technologies and CAE Inc.) into actionable legal and technical tax architecture, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how Canadian corporations facing identical public-sector funding structures can proactively restructure their contractual terms, corporate and project governance, technical documentation, and financial accounting to preserve their SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.
Case Study 1: Clean-Tech Bitumen and Hydrogen Co-Processing Joint Venture with a Provincial Crown Agency
Industry Context and the CCLC Technologies Pitfall Scenario

Alberta SynCatalyst Corp. ("SynCatalyst") is a Calgary-based Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation ("CCPC") developing a novel plasma-catalytic reactor designed to co-process heavy Athabasca bitumen and agricultural biomass into low-carbon synthetic light crude and turquoise hydrogen. For its current taxation year, SynCatalyst budgets $4,500,000 in qualifying SR&ED wages, contractor fees, and materials consumed in experimental trials, anticipating an enhanced 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC on the full amount, which falls within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (with 15% applying to any excess), pursuant to subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(1) of the Act.

To finance the construction of a pilot scale-up unit and associated bench-scale catalyst testing, SynCatalyst negotiates a "Bitumen Co-Processing Technology Development Agreement" with a provincial Crown agency ("Alberta CleanTech Authority" or "ACTA"), a public authority under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ii) and subsection 127(9). Under the initial draft agreement, ACTA agrees to contribute $3,500,000 over 18 months to reimburse 75% of SynCatalyst's eligible project costs, covering both core laboratory SR&ED and commercial engineering validation. SynCatalyst and ACTA pool background patents and take an interim 50/50 undivided co-ownership interest in all foreground intellectual property. Upon achieving "Commercial Readiness" (defined as 500 hours of continuous pilot operation), ACTA is contractually obligated to assign its 50% IP interest to SynCatalyst in exchange for a 5% gross revenue royalty that terminates automatically once ACTA recovers its $3,500,000 principal plus prime plus 1% interest. Furthermore, a Joint Technical Steering Committee (with two ACTA appointees and two SynCatalyst executives) approves quarterly test protocols and holds authority to suspend funding if SynCatalyst's working capital ratio falls below 1.2:1.

If executed as drafted, the CRA will audit the claim and disallow SynCatalyst's refundable ITCs on $3,500,000 of expenditures. Under CCLC Technologies, ACTA's mandatory buy-out capped at principal plus nominal interest means ACTA can earn no net commercial profit upon success, while bearing full downside exposure if the technology fails to commercialize. The 50/50 interim IP ownership will fail subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) because ACTA acquires no lasting property rights in a going concern, and the Joint Technical Steering Committee will be dismissed as the surveillance of a "prudent grant-giver".
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring of Consideration, Equity, and Repayment Mechanics

To neutralize subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv) and subsection 127(9), SynCatalyst's tax counsel must eliminate the hybrid "capped buy-back co-ownership" model and restructure the $3,500,000 public funding into one of three legally compliant architectures. Under the first architecture—a true commercial equity subscription under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) acquiring lasting property rights in a going concern—instead of advancing project-expense reimbursements linked to defeasible IP co-ownership, ACTA subscribes for $3,500,000 of Class B Preferred or Common Shares in the capital stock of SynCatalyst (or subscribes for units in a dedicated commercial Joint Venture corporation). To satisfy the Federal Court of Appeal's test in Paragraph 7 of CCLC Technologies and CRA administrative policy, the parties must completely eliminate any mandatory capped buy-back obligating ACTA to sell its shares or IP interest back to SynCatalyst for principal plus interest upon commercialization. Instead, the shares issued to ACTA must confer enduring upside participation through genuine commercial attributes, including the right to participate in uncapped dividends, enterprise value appreciation, and a fair-market-value ("FMV") put/call redemption right priced via an independent third-party valuation at the time of exercise rather than a pre-fixed cost-recovery cap. Moreover, the Share Subscription Agreement must stipulate that the $3,500,000 is paid strictly as capital consideration for the issuance of treasury shares in the corporation (acquiring a lasting interest in the taxpayer's business under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii)), with no covenant tying disbursements to the reimbursement of specific SR&ED expense line items under subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv).

Under the second alternative architecture—an unconditional, bona fide repayable loan structure—if ACTA's enabling statute prohibits holding permanent corporate equity, the funding agreement must be converted from a revenue-contingent royalty contribution into a bona fide loan with unconditional repayment obligations. Counsel must remove all contingencies tying repayment to "Commercial Readiness" or gross revenue royalties and establish a fixed, unconditional maturity schedule requiring full-recourse repayment of the $3,500,000 principal over a defined amortization period (such as 8 years following a fixed 24-month grace period), regardless of whether the plasma-catalytic process succeeds or fails commercially. The loan instrument must include enforceable creditor remedies upon default, contain no automatic forgiveness provisions, and satisfy the post-CAE Inc. statutory criteria enacted by Parliament for bona fide repayable government loans (the "excluded loan" definition in subsection 12(11), added by the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1, assented to June 20, 2024) so that the principal is excluded from paragraph 12(1)(x) and subsection 127(9).

Under the third alternative architecture—contractual ring-fencing of assistance to non-SR&ED capital and commercialization costs—if ACTA insists on providing a non-repayable grant or revenue-contingent contribution, SynCatalyst must contractually allocate 100% of ACTA's $3,500,000 funding exclusively to non-SR&ED project activities. Because capital expenditures qualify for SR&ED ITCs only where they are made on SR&ED carried on in Canada, and because commercial plant engineering, environmental permitting, market studies, and balance-of-plant construction fall outside the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, the funding contract's Schedule of Eligible Expenditures must explicitly restrict ACTA's $3,500,000 reimbursement strictly to physical pilot-plant capital asset fabrication, site civil works, and commercial certification, expressly prohibiting any allocation of ACTA funds toward the $4,500,000 in bench-scale SR&ED salaries and experimental consumables.
Step 2: Realigning Project Governance and Technical Committee Mandates

To overcome the "prudent grant-giver" presumption articulated by Justice Strayer in Paragraph 6 of CCLC Technologies, SynCatalyst must overhaul its project governance. Where the commercial equity or joint venture structure is selected, the parties must replace the Project Management Committee's expense-reimbursement vetting and working-capital withholding clauses (which mirror Paragraph 5(6) of CCLC's agreement) with standard corporate Shareholder Agreement governance. ACTA should appoint a director or observer to SynCatalyst's Board of Directors exercising fiduciary oversight over corporate strategy rather than auditing individual R&D timesheets as a grant administrator. Contemporaneous Board and Commercial Committee minutes should record that ACTA's technical personnel are contributing proprietary bitumen assay databases and licensing foreground IP to third-party provincial upgraders for uncapped commercial licensing fees shared 50/50—demonstrating an active, profit-seeking commercial business purpose under Consumers' Gas.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and SR&ED Eligibility Segregation

SynCatalyst's engineering and tax advisors must simultaneously restructure the technical project architecture to prevent any residual assistance from contaminating the core SR&ED claim. Instead of filing a single, monolithic "Bitumen Co-Processing Project" on CRA Form T661—which allows assistance in one area to grind down the entire project's qualified expenditures under subsections 127(18) and 127(19)—SynCatalyst must divide the technical work into two distinct, standalone projects with separate technological baselines and work breakdown structures. The first project (Project 101: Unassisted Core SR&ED — Plasma-Catalyst Deactivation Kinetics) must focus purely on resolving fundamental technological uncertainties regarding coking suppression and catalyst pore-structure degradation under high-sulfur bitumen partial pressure, with zero ACTA funds requested, budgeted, or permitted. The second project (Project 102: Assisted Commercial Scale-Up & Balance-of-Plant Engineering) must encompass the mechanical integration, pressure-vessel fabrication, and environmental emissions scrubbing funded by ACTA. Within Project 101, engineering leads must maintain dated laboratory notebooks, gas-chromatography run logs, and failed catalyst formulation records that explicitly map every experimental iteration to a specific technological uncertainty, isolating the systematic investigation from the commercial demonstration milestones governed by the ACTA agreement.
Step 4: Experimentation Cost Tracking and Accrual Accounting Controls

At the accounting level, SynCatalyst must establish separate ERP general ledger cost centers (CC-101-SRED versus CC-102-ACTA-CAPEX). Timecards for Ph.D. chemical engineers and metallurgists performing systematic experimentation under Project 101 must be billed exclusively to CC-101-SRED, while vendor invoices for pilot plant structural steel and commercial engineering reimbursed by ACTA are booked exclusively to CC-102-ACTA-CAPEX. Under subsection 127(18) and the CRA's accrual policy, any assistance a claimant is "entitled to receive" at year-end reduces qualified expenditures immediately. By ensuring that ACTA's claim submissions and milestone certificates reference only CC-102-ACTA-CAPEX invoices, any year-end receivable from ACTA is legally and factually "in respect of" non-SR&ED capital and commercial expenditures, leaving the $4,500,000 pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures in CC-101-SRED 100% intact for the 35% refundable ITC.

Uncapped preferred/common equity subscription at FMV or unconditional full-recourse repayable loan or non-SR&ED CapEx ring-fencing.
Satisfies Consumers' Gas / CCLC ordinary business test & s. 12(1)(x)(viii) lasting property rights standard.
Governance & Oversight Mechanics
Joint Committee vetting R&D expense claims with Paragraph 5(6) solvency withholding rights.
Corporate Board seat / Shareholder Agreement governance focused on enterprise value and uncapped IP licensing.
Neutralizes Justice Strayer's "prudent grant-giver" presumption in Paragraph 6 of CCLC Technologies.

Single combined R&D and pilot-plant project on Form T661.
Bifurcated Project 101 (Unassisted Bench SR&ED) and Project 102 (Assisted Balance-of-Plant CapEx).
Prevents cross-project assistance grind under subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the Act.
General Ledger & Accrual Tracking
Commingled project ledger accruing year-end ACTA receivables against SR&ED labour.
Segregated ERP cost centers (CC-101-SRED vs. CC-102-ACTA-CAPEX) with strict invoice mapping.
Isolates year-end receivables from qualified SR&ED expenditures under s. 127(9) and s. 127(18).

body.text: Case Study 2: Aerospace and Dual-Use Sensor Development Under a Federal Public Authority Contribution Agreement
Industry Context and the CCLC Technologies Pitfall Scenario

Borealis Photonics Inc. ("Borealis") is an Ottawa-based aerospace and defence technology corporation developing a solid-state quantum-photonic LiDAR and synthetic aperture radar ("SAR") sensor suite for autonomous arctic surveillance aircraft. In its current taxation year, Borealis incurs $6,000,000 in current SR&ED expenditures (engineering salaries and specialized cleanroom semiconductor fabrication subcontracts) under paragraph 37(1)(a).

Borealis enters into a multi-year "Strategic Sensor Technology Contribution Agreement" with a federal public authority department ("Federal Innovation Agency" or "FIA"). Under the initial contract terms, FIA provides $4,000,000 in milestone-based financial contributions during the taxation year, comprising $2,000,000 paid in cash during the year and $2,000,000 accrued upon completion of Milestone 4 on December 20, just prior to Borealis's December 31 fiscal year-end. Paragraph 18 of the agreement states that "nothing herein creates a partnership or joint venture". To avoid "grant" optics, the agreement characterizes the $4,000,000 as a "Pre-Commercial Technology Co-Investment" whereby the Crown acquires an undivided 40% beneficial interest in the foreground photonic circuit IP. However, Schedule B stipulates that upon Borealis achieving Transport Canada and Department of National Defence ("DND") flight-readiness certification, Borealis has an automatic right and obligation to redeem the Crown's 40% IP interest by repaying the $4,000,000 principal in 10 equal annual installments bearing 0% interest, plus a one-time 2% administrative fee. If flight-readiness certification is never achieved, Borealis owes nothing, and the Crown retains its 40% interest in the uncertified sensor IP. Meanwhile, FIA's technical directorate conducts bi-monthly design reviews and must pre-approve any changes to the sensor's technical specifications.

This initial structure replicates every fatal flaw of CCLC Technologies, as well as Immunovaccine and CAE Inc.. First, the Crown's 0%-interest, capped redemption upon certification yields zero net commercial profit to the Crown while exposing it to total capital loss if certification fails—failing the Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies ordinary business arrangement test. Second, the Crown's 40% IP interest vanishes upon commercial success, disqualifying the payments from the subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) property acquisition exemption. Third, if Borealis argues in the alternative that the payments represent commercial procurement, the CRA will classify the $4,000,000 as a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) (an amount payable by a Canadian government or public authority for SR&ED to be performed "for it or on its behalf"), which reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) just as severely as government assistance. Finally, the $2,000,000 December 20 receivable will be swept into the current year's ITC reduction on an accrual basis.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring — Distinguishing Commercial Goods Procurement from SR&ED Assistance and Contract Payments

Borealis must restructure the legal nature of the transaction so that the public authority's payments constitute neither "government assistance" (subsection 127(9)) nor a "contract payment" for SR&ED performed on the government's behalf (subsection 127(9)). Where FIA or an affiliated defence ministry actually requires sensor hardware for its own operational fleet, tax counsel should convert the "Technology Contribution Agreement" into a fixed-price Commercial Goods Purchase Agreement for the delivery of finished, flight-tested surveillance pods at a specified future date, while Borealis retains 100% ownership of all background and foreground IP. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, a payment from a Canadian government body is not a "contract payment" that reduces SR&ED ITCs if the contract is in substance for the purchase of a commercial deliverable or good rather than a contract "for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf". To establish this substantive distinction, the contract must stipulate a fixed commercial price for the physical delivery of specified hardware units (placing genuine commercial profit and cost-overrun risk on Borealis), contain no covenant requiring Borealis to perform specific SR&ED tasks or reimburse R&D labour hours, vest 100% of all intellectual property rights solely in Borealis (eliminating the illusory 40% Crown IP co-ownership and buy-back that failed in CCLC Technologies), and price the hardware units at arm's-length commercial market rates. Because the government payor receives tangible operational radar hardware for its fleet at a fixed commercial price, the payment is made to advance the operational business and procurement interests of the payor for full consideration, removing any colour of a grant or subsidy under Consumers' Gas and CCLC Technologies.

Conversely, if the funding comes purely from an economic development agency (such as FIA under an innovation contribution program) that does not procure operational hardware, Borealis must eliminate the 40% IP co-ownership and buy-back artifice and execute an Unconditional Repayable Loan Agreement. Counsel must remove the condition linking repayment to Transport Canada or DND flight-readiness certification, because under CCLC Technologies, any clause that leaves the government holding uncommercialized IP instead of cash repayment when commercialization fails converts the instrument into a forgivable loan or subsidy. The $4,000,000 loan must be made unconditionally repayable on a fixed schedule with full corporate recourse against Borealis, structured specifically to qualify under the statutory carve-out for bona fide repayable government loans so that neither subsection 127(9) government assistance nor paragraph 12(1)(x) income inclusion applies.
Step 2: Governance and Milestone Architecture

To insulate the project from the "prudent grant-giver" finding in CCLC Technologies and prevent "contract payment" characterization under subsection 127(9), Borealis must decouple customer acceptance reviews from R&D methodology control. Under the fixed-price hardware supply pathway, the agreement must strip the government agency of any contractual right to sit on an internal R&D steering committee or dictate how the experimental semiconductor fabrication is conducted. The government's technical interaction must be restricted strictly to standard customer acceptance testing—verifying that the delivered prototype pod meets external form-fit-and-function interface specifications upon delivery. As recognized in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a public payer controls how SR&ED work is performed or reimburses R&D inputs rather than paying for a finished commercial output upon acceptance, the risk of "contract payment" or "prudent grant-giver" recharacterization escalates sharply. Additionally, counsel must eliminate contradictory boilerplate clauses (such as Paragraph 18 in CCLC Technologies) so that the contract's operative provisions, IP ownership clauses, and general terms are 100% aligned with either an arm's-length vendor-purchaser supply contract or a debtor-creditor unconditional loan agreement.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Technological Uncertainty and Systematic Investigation

To ensure the $6,000,000 in internal SR&ED expenditures withstands rigorous CRA Research and Technology Advisor ("RTA") and Financial Reviewer scrutiny, Borealis must segregate customer acceptance testing from core SR&ED in its contemporaneous technical records. The technical file must document that while the government supply contract requires delivery of an integrated sensor unit meeting specified external performance metrics, the decision to undertake fundamental SR&ED into quantum-photonic waveguide phase-noise suppression was initiated internally by Borealis to advance its proprietary corporate technology platform. Engineering directors must compile a structured SR&ED technical evidence package containing three core elements: first, engineering literature reviews and baseline simulations proving that standard gallium-arsenide photonic waveguides cannot maintain phase coherence below 0.5° RMS phase error under high-vibration aircraft profiles (establishing technological uncertainty); second, dated cleanroom wafer fabrication logs, thermal-vacuum chamber test telemetry, and iterative algorithmic signal-processing models demonstrating a systematic investigation from hypothesis generation through empirical testing to logical conclusion; and third, quantitative test reports documenting the exact technological advancement achieved regarding sub-micron waveguide geometry, even on experimental runs that failed to achieve target signal-to-noise ratios (reaffirming that SR&ED eligibility depends on technological advancement rather than commercial success, whereas CCLC Technologies demonstrates that commercial failure turns contingent government funding into assistance).
Step 4: Financial Tracking, Accrual Timing, and Repayment Planning

In CCLC Technologies, $1,564,748 of the $2,290,317 assistance reduction had not even been received in cash in 1987, but was swept into the reassessment because it was receivable at year-end. If Borealis utilizes any form of government assistance for a segregated non-SR&ED sub-project, its financial controllers must track the exact timing of when contractual conditions precedent are fulfilled. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, an amount becomes "entitled to be received" only when the claimant has fulfilled all contractual conditions precedent to create an enforceable legal right to payment.

Furthermore, if Borealis ever accepts a conditionally repayable contribution for a discrete work package, tax counsel must model the multi-year cash-flow and tax-rate asymmetry upfront: the assistance will reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) in the year it becomes receivable, and any future repayment made if the project succeeds will only restore the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (and generate ITCs under paragraphs (e.1) and (e.2) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9)) in the subsequent taxation year in which the repayment is actually made. Because a CCPC loses access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, together with that of associated corporations, exceeds the $15 million to $75 million phase-out range in subsection 127(10.2) for that future repayment year, preserving upfront eligibility via an unconditional bona fide loan or commercial hardware supply structure (avoiding the CCLC Technologies trap at inception) is vastly superior to relying on subsequent paragraph 37(1)(c) repayment deductions.

Prevents recharacterization as SR&ED performed "for or on behalf of" the Crown under s. 127(9).

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Her Majesty the Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 DTC 6527) remains a watershed authority in Canadian tax law. It dismantled the notion that taxpayers and public authorities can disguise government grants, subsidies, or conditionally repayable contributions as commercial joint ventures or property acquisitions through formalistic conveyancing labels. Three enduring legal principles govern all Canadian SR&ED tax planning in the wake of CCLC Technologies. First, economic asymmetry defeats commercial animus: a public funding arrangement under which the government payor cannot receive any net profit if the venture succeeds, and gains only an equity interest if the venture proves uncommercial, is not an ordinary business arrangement under Consumers' Gas and, in the circumstances of non-commercialization, constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subparagraph 12(1)(x)(iv). Second, defeasible title defeats subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii): granting a government body an interim co-ownership interest in R&D intellectual property or corporate equity will not qualify for the property acquisition exclusion in subparagraph 12(1)(x)(viii) if a mandatory buy-back or redemption clause strips the government of lasting property rights in a going concern upon commercialization in exchange for a capped return of principal and interest. Third, oversight does not equate to commercial partnership: technical surveillance, steering committee participation, and financial withholding covenants exercised by government representatives are at least equally consistent with the role of a "prudent grant-giver" and do not, in themselves, indicate any commercial role of the government. By rigorously applying these principles during the contract drafting stage—prior to executing public funding agreements or incurring SR&ED expenditures—Canadian tax counsel and technical advisors can structure bona fide equity subscriptions, compliant unconditional loans, or ring-fenced commercial procurement contracts that fully safeguard the taxpayer's entitlement to federal and provincial SR&ED tax incentives.
